abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Background: Autobiographical memory theory suggests that how stressful events are encoded and recalled, particularly in terms of centrality to identity, emotional intensity, and retrieval frequency, can influence mental health. In breast cancer care, the disclosure of biopsy results may represent a psychologically impactful moment, regardless of diagnosis type.

Objectives: This mixed-method study aimed to determine whether and how narrative features of breast biopsy result disclosure, analysed by both content (what was said) and form (how it was said), are associated with psychological distress one month later.

Method: Sixty-eight participants were interviewed ≥7 days after receiving a breast biopsy result. Psychological distress was assessed one month later using the Distress Thermometer (non-specific distress) and the Impact of Event Scale–Revised (post-traumatic stress symptoms; PTSS). Narratives were coded using a theory-driven framework assessing centrality, emotional intensity, and recall frequency, applied separately to content and form.

Results: While controlling for self-reported dissociation, linear regressions showed that for content, centrality and emotional intensity were significantly associated with PTSS, whereas only emotional intensity was significantly associated with non-specific distress. No substantial evidence of an association was found between frequency and any psychological outcome. In terms of form, all three dimensions were significantly associated to PTSS, while frequency and emotional intensity were significantly associated with non-specific distress. Early narrative markers following breast biopsy result disclosure were associated with psychological distress one month later.

Conclusions: These findings highlight how memory processes associated with medical stressors can shape psychological outcomes and support their potential as screening tools for early identification of at-risk individuals.

list-item.p: Autobiographical narratives of breast biopsy results disclosure show early markers of psychological distress measured throughout non-specific distress and post-traumatic stress symptoms.
How biopsy disclosure is narrated reveals psychological distress beyond standard screening tools used in oncology.
Brief narrative prompts may help identify patients at risk for later distress.

trans-abstract.p: Antecedentes: La teoría de la memoria autobiográfica sugiere que la manera en que se codifican y recuerdan los acontecimientos estresantes, particularmente en términos de centralidad para la identidad, intensidad emocional y frecuencia de evocación, puede influir en la salud mental. En el contexto del cáncer de mama, la comunicación de los resultados de una biopsia puede representar un momento de gran impacto psicológico, independientemente del tipo de diagnóstico.

Objetivo: Este estudio de métodos mixtos tuvo como objetivo determinar si las características narrativas de la comunicación de los resultados de una biopsia mamaria, analizadas tanto en términos de contenido (lo que se dijo) como de forma (cómo se dijo), se asociaban con el malestar psicológico un mes después.

Método: Se entrevistaron a sesenta y ocho participantes ≥7 días después de recibir el resultado de una biopsia mamaria. El malestar psicológico se evaluó un mes más tarde mediante el Termómetro de Distrés (malestar inespecífico) y la Escala de Impacto del Evento–Revisada (síntomas de estrés postraumático; SEPT). Las narrativas se codificaron mediante un marco de análisis fundamentado teóricamente que evaluó la centralidad, la intensidad emocional y la frecuencia de recuerdo, aplicado por separado al contenido y a la forma.

Resultados: Controlando la disociación autorreportada, las regresiones lineales mostraron que, en cuanto al contenido, la centralidad y la intensidad emocional se asociaron significativamente con los SEPT, mientras que solo la intensidad emocional se asoció significativamente con el malestar inespecífico. No se encontró evidencia sustancial de asociación entre la frecuencia y ninguno de los desenlaces psicológicos. En cuanto a la forma, las tres dimensiones se asociaron significativamente con los SEPT, mientras que la frecuencia y la intensidad emocional se asociaron significativamente con el malestar inespecífico. Los marcadores narrativos tempranos tras la comunicación del resultado de la biopsia mamaria se asociaron con el malestar psicológico un mes después.

Conclusión: Estos hallazgos ponen de relieve cómo los procesos de memoria asociados con estresores médicos pueden influir en los resultados psicológicos y respaldan su potencial como herramientas de detección para la identificación temprana de personas en riesgo.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Thousands of women undergo breast biopsies each year following routine screening or the detection of a potential abnormality (Siegel et al., 2025). Biopsy is the only procedure that enables confirmation of a breast cancer diagnosis, making it a critical point in the medical trajectory (American Cancer Society, 2024). This phase is often marked by heightened emotional vulnerability and health-related uncertainty, as it confronts individuals with the possibility of a life-threatening illness (Andrykowski et al., 2002; Fortin, Rudd, et al., 2025). Biopsy result disclosure, regardless of whether the outcome is positive (malignant) or negative (benign or no breast condition), can trigger strong emotional responses, as individuals confront either a life-altering diagnosis or lingering fears despite reassuring news (Andrykowski et al., 2002; Brewer et al., 2007; Fortin et al., 2021). Importantly, up to one third of patients report persisting psychological distress symptoms following result disclosure, regardless of diagnosis, and such subclinical manifestations impair daily functioning and quality of life (Fortin, Paquin, et al., 2025; Fortin, Rudd, et al., 2025; Steffens et al., 2011).

In psycho-oncology, psychological distress is a central concern as it can range from transient, adaptive reactions to persistent and impairing symptoms, and has even been described as the ‘sixth vital sign,’ underscoring its importance alongside traditional medical indicators such as blood pressure, temperature, pulse, respiration, and pain (Bultz et al., 2011; Deshields et al., 2021). Among the possible manifestations, post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) and non-specific distress represent the most severe forms of cancer-related psychological distress, as both, when persistent and unaddressed, are linked to psychiatric morbidity and long-term functional impairment (Cordova et al., 2017; Kangas et al., 2002; National Comprehensive Cancer Network, 2003). Indeed, PTSS are typically triggered by discrete, emotionally charged events, such as the disclosure of a diagnosis (Cordova et al., 2017; Kangas et al., 2002). These PTSS include intrusive recollections (e.g. recurrent thoughts about cancer), avoidance (e.g. avoiding cancer-related discussions), negative alterations in mood (e.g. persistent fear or sadness) and cognition (e.g. difficulty envisioning a positive future), and hyperarousal (e.g. increased monitoring or examination of the breast) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Non-specific distress, by contrast, is generally defined as a negative emotional and cognitive reaction to illness without mapping onto a formal psychiatric diagnosis (National Comprehensive Cancer Network, 2003). It is the most widely used indicator of psychological vulnerability in oncology, supported by international guidelines and embedded in routine psychosocial screening through tools such as the Distress Thermometer (National Comprehensive Cancer Network, 2003). Since PTSS and non-specific distress capture different aspects of psychological adjustment (Fortin, Paquin, et al., 2025; Fortin, Rudd, et al., 2025) and can both evolve into debilitating conditions, identifying early predictors of each is crucial to guide preventive care.

This emotionally charged event around the time of result disclosure may influence how the experience is encoded into memory. According to the memory consolidation theory (McGaugh, 1966), novel experiences are initially encoded in short-term memory and gradually stabilized in long-term memory through a biochemical process that unfolds over several days, typically completing within a week (Gisquet-Verrier & Riccio, 2022; Przybyslawski et al., 1999). When the event is perceived as highly stressful, heightened noradrenergic activity can lead to overconsolidation, making the memory more vivid and persistent (Pitman, 1989; Southwick et al., 2002). The emotionally salient nature of such events increases hippocampal and amygdala activity (Kukolja et al., 2011), which in turn strengthen long-term memory formation (Van Stegeren, 2008), and may increase vulnerability to psychological distress (Giffard et al., 2013; Kangas et al., 2005). Although encoding and consolidation are typically strengthened for emotional events, they can nonetheless be hindered by peritraumatic dissociation. This acute reaction, which may occur within 24 h following an emotionally overwhelming event, is often described as a temporary sense of detachment or unreality (Bedard-Gilligan & Zoellner, 2012; Van der Kolk & Fisler, 1995). Rather than enhancing memory salience, dissociation may dampen attention and emotional engagement at the time of encoding, resulting in memories that are less fully consolidated (Bedard-Gilligan & Zoellner, 2012; Mattos et al., 2016; Van der Kolk & Fisler, 1995).

Building on this framework, autobiographical memories formed in the wake of significant medical stressors, such as receiving biopsy results, may acquire lasting salience due to their emotional charge and personal relevance. Autobiographical memory is the system by which individuals encode and recall personal experiences, anchoring them in time, place, and self-relevance (Conway et al., 2005; Tulving et al., 1988). This system combines episodic elements (i.e. sensory and perceptual representations of specific events) with semantic self-knowledge (i.e. factual knowledge about the self like profession or age) (Haslam et al., 2011; Piolino et al., 2000). According to Rubin and Umanath (2015), three dimensions of autobiographical memory are particularly relevant in the context of stressful or traumatic events: emotional intensity, retrieval frequency, and centrality to one’s identity. Through enhanced consolidation, these characteristics increase the likelihood that distressing events will be deeply encoded and persistently recalled over time (Rubin & Berntsen, 2009).

To our knowledge, no study in the breast cancer trajectory has examined the specific characteristics of illness-related autobiographical memories in terms of their centrality, emotional intensity, and recall frequency. This gap may reflect the fact that memories collected during or after treatment can be altered by side effects, particularly chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment (Martino et al., 2023; Nilsson-Ihrfelt et al., 2004; Sebri et al., 2020). Yet the pre-treatment phase offers a unique opportunity to investigate these autobiographical memory mechanisms as predictors of subsequent psychological distress, rather than limiting their study to markers of severity once survivorship has been reached. Prior studies, mostly conducted in individuals living with a post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) diagnosis, have shown that specific features of autobiographical narratives content are closely linked to psychological outcomes (Ayers et al., 2015; Crespo & Fernández-Lansac, 2016; Kindt et al., 2007; Tani et al., 2016). In stressful contexts, the way individuals recall and structure their memories can reflect unresolved emotional and cognitive processing. For instance, when an event is perceived as central to one’s identity, but narrated in a fragmented, distanced or incoherent way, it often signals psychological distress (Ayers et al., 2015). Centrality is especially relevant because experiences deeply integrated into the self-concept may disrupt one’s sense of identity and continuity if left unresolved, increasing vulnerability to mental health issues (Berntsen & Rubin, 2007). Additionally, intense emotional expression, including negative affect, dissociation, and highly detailed, vivid and specific descriptions, has been associated with greater trauma symptoms (Bisson Desrochers et al., 2016; Foa et al., 1995; Kindt et al., 2007; Pennebaker et al., 2001; Rubin & Umanath, 2015). Importantly, dissociative features coded within trauma narratives, such as fragmented or incoherent recall, have been linked to subsequent symptomatology, more reliably than dissociation assessed through self-report questionnaires (Bedard-Gilligan & Zoellner, 2012). Sustained emotional intensity in memory recall can interfere with emotional regulation and is a known precursor of various psychological disorders when not properly addressed (see review: Rybak-Korneluk et al., 2016). Furthermore, frequent memory retrieval, whether voluntary or intrusive, may reflect persistent cognitive engagement with the event, and difficulty achieving closure (Rubin & Umanath, 2015). Repeated recollection can maintain psychological distress over time by keeping the emotional and cognitive salience of the event active, especially in the absence of adaptive meaning-making processes (Rubin & Berntsen, 2009). Taken together, these narrative characteristics highlight how content of memory recall can serve as markers of unresolved emotional processing and psychological vulnerability, which is observed in both types of biopsy results (positive and negative).

Beyond content, the form of autobiographical narratives, how the story is conveyed, can also shape psychological outcomes. Narrative centrality can be reflected in linguistic markers of self-reference, such as the frequent use of first-person singular pronouns (e.g. I, me, my), which have been associated with greater PTSS severity. A self-immersed narrative style may signal difficulties in gaining perspective on the event and contribute to heightened emotional reactivity over time (Kleim et al., 2018; Pennebaker et al., 2001). Emotional intensity, in turn, can be inferred from paralinguistic and linguistic features, such as negative affective tone, verbal fillers, and lexical repetitions. These markers suggest deeper emotional engagement and may reflect ongoing cognitive disorganization or difficulty regulating affect in response to the memory (Kennedy-Moore & Watson, 2001). Finally, narrative recall frequency can indirectly be indexed through the density of event-related vocabulary, for instance, in a medical context, references to illness. A higher concentration of such terms may point to persistent preoccupation with the event and sustained activation of the memory trace (see review: Papini et al., 2015; Quillivic et al., 2025).

Despite these advances, no study to date, to our knowledge, has examined the narrative recall of the breast biopsy result disclosure, a potentially emotionally charged and stressful event central to the cancer trajectory, as an early indicator of psychological distress. While narrative features have mostly been used in the context of PTSD, either as correlates of symptom severity once the diagnosis is established (see reviews: Crespo & Fernández-Lansac, 2016; O’Kearney & Perrott, 2006) or to evaluate the efficacy of psychosocial interventions (e.g. see review: Raeder et al., 2023), their potential value for identifying early vulnerability and preventing both PTSS and non-specific distress remains underexplored, especially in oncology. By assessing how individuals recall and communicate this critical moment shortly after it occurs, the present study positions narrative analysis not as a therapeutic endpoint, but as a potential preventive tool, one that may help identify those at greater risk for distress before symptoms fully emerge.

sec.title: Aims and hypotheses
sec.p: The present study aimed to examine whether and how three autobiographical narrative dimensions – centrality, emotional intensity, and recall frequency – in both the content and form of participants’ memory of their breast biopsy result disclosure (recalled after seven days post-biopsy disclosure) were associated with psychological distress (PTSS and non-specific distress) one month later. It was hypothesized that higher levels of these three narrative dimensions would be associated with greater psychological distress in both content and form.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The present study draws from a larger longitudinal research project examining biopsychosocial predictors of psychological distress and quality of life following a breast biopsy, with data collected at seven time points. Data from this longitudinal project have already been used to examine peritraumatic distress as a predictor of trauma-related symptoms (Fortin, Paquin, et al., 2025). For the current analyses, we included only participants who accepted and were available to participate in an optional narrative interview (i.e. an open-ended interview in which participants recount a personally experienced event with minimal interviewer interruption; Kaźmierska, 2004) following the disclosure of their biopsy results and who also completed the psychological distress questionnaires one-month post-diagnosis. Of the 209 participants enrolled in the larger longitudinal study, 98 (46.9%) agreed to participate in the optional narrative interview. Among those who did not ultimately complete the interview, most were unavailable within the required post-disclosure timeframe (85.2%), whereas a smaller proportion later declined participation (14.8%). Preliminary analyses (independent-samples t-tests and chi-square tests) indicated that participants who completed the narrative interview did not differ significantly from those who did not on sociodemographic or clinical characteristics, except that a history of a diagnosed mental health disorder was less common among participants of the present subsample (p = .007). Ethics approval was obtained from the Centre intégré universitaire de santé et de services sociaux (CIUSSS) de l’Est-de-l’Île-de-Montréal (CEMTL- 2024–3378).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Recruitment took place between June 2023 and October 2024 at the specialized Breast Clinic of Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital, in close collaboration with the medical team (oncologists and nurses). Potential participants were either introduced to the study in person following the prescription of a breast biopsy, during a clinic visit where they received an informational brochure, or were later contacted by phone if they had expressed interest through their healthcare provider. Eligibility criteria included: (i) being 18 years of age or older, regardless of gender; (ii) currently undergoing or awaiting the results of a breast biopsy; (iii) fluency in spoken and written French; and (iv) the capacity to give free and informed consent. Individuals were excluded if they (i) had a diagnosis of another type of cancer, (ii) presented an imminent suicide risk, or (iii) reported a severe mental health or neurological condition likely to interfere with consent. These exclusion criteria were assessed by the medical team during routine clinical care prior to referral to the study. To be eligible for the optional narrative interview, participants were also required to have access to a telephone, tablet, or computer to complete the interview remotely, which was confirmed by the research team during study enrolment (this criterion did not result in the exclusion of any potential participants).

At T1 (biopsy prescription), participants were recruited, signed the consent form and then completed the sociodemographic questionnaire. At T2 (biopsy results disclosure), the research team monitored the hospital’s electronic medical system daily to identify biopsy result appointments in real time. Within 24 h following the results disclosure, patients completed The Peritraumatic Dissociative Experience Questionnaire (PDEQ-10SRV). At T3 (seven days post-disclosure), participants who had agreed to take part in the optional narrative interview were invited to recount their experience of receiving the biopsy results. These interviews were conducted, on average, 15 days post-disclosure (M = 15.00, SD = 3.80; range = 9–26 days). Interviews were scheduled by phone and conducted via Zoom (Gray et al., 2020), with participants choosing between phone call (via Zoom), video with or without their camera, and whether the interviewer’s camera would be turned on. Interviews were conducted by either JF (N = 30 interviews) or AP (N = 41 interviews), two trained researchers who were randomly assigned to participants by a third team member [RL] based on availability. For each session, a personalized Zoom link and password were emailed to participants, and the waiting room function was enabled to control access. Once the session began, the meeting was locked to prevent unauthorized entry. Interviews lasted between 20 and 60 min and were audio-recorded to facilitate transcription and analysis. Each recording was transcribed verbatim capturing word-for-word content including hesitations, repetitions, pauses, slang, and speech errors. Transcriptions were then reviewed by the original interviewer to ensure completeness and strengthen accuracy. At T4 (one-month post-biopsy results), participants completed the self-report measures of psychological distress (i.e. the Impact of Event Scale-Revised and the Distress Thermometer). Questionnaires were administered online or in paper format based on participants’ preference.

sec.title: Qualitative
sec.p: Interview guide. The interview guide included a sequence of open-ended questions designed to elicit autobiographical narratives related to the experience of biopsy result disclosure. The interview began with the Test Épisodique de Mémoire du Passé Autobiographique (TEMPau; Piolino et al., 2000), used to assess baseline narrative specificity and memory features in which participants recalled autobiographical events that were personally significant to them over the past five years but that occurred more than one week prior to the interview. Specifically, they were asked to recall four events: (1) a meaningful encounter, (2) a significant work-related event, (3) a memorable day during a trip, and (4) a family-related event. To facilitate retrieval, concrete examples were provided for each category (e.g. new friend/worker; retirement celebration; cabin, camping; or birthday, wedding, Christmas), as such cues are known to enhance access to specific autobiographical memories (Piolino et al., 2000). The number of events recalled ranged from one to four across participants. When participants were unable to recall an event or reported an experience that was too recent (less than seven days prior) or too distant (more than five years prior), the event was excluded from analyses. The baseline autobiographical events questions were followed by questions adapted from Ayers et al. (2015), originally developed to explore narrative recall following stressful or traumatic events. Participants were asked to confirm the type of biopsy results they had received (positive/negative), then were invited to describe, in as much details as possible, what occurred on the day of the result disclosure, from the moment they woke up until the time that they received the official biopsy result. The interview guide included additional follow-up questions for broader research objectives, but these were excluded, and analyses focused solely on the narrative of the biopsy results disclosure experience.

sec.title: Quantitative
sec.p: Sociodemographic data. Sociodemographic information was collected through the initial questionnaire completed by participants at the time of biopsy prescription.

Psychological distress. Post-traumatic stress symptoms were measured using the validated French version of the Impact of Event Scale-Revised (IES-R; Brunet et al., 2003; Weiss & Marmar, 1996), which evaluates distress associated with a specific traumatic event. Participants were instructed to respond in reference to the biopsy result disclosure. The 22 items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely), with possible scores ranging from 0 to 88. The questionnaire has shown excellent internal consistency (α = .94). Non-specific distress was assessed with the French version of the Distress Thermometer (National Comprehensive Cancer Network, 2003), a single-item scale ranging from 0 (no distress) to 10 (extreme distress) (Ownby, 2019). This questionnaire has been validated in different countries and in multiple oncologic populations, including breast cancer (Donovan et al., 2014). For both self-report questionnaires, higher scores indicate greater symptom severity.

Dissociation. Self-reported dissociation was measured within 24 h following the biopsy result disclosure with the validated French version of The Peritraumatic Dissociative Experience Questionnaire (PDEQ-10SRV; Birmes et al., 2005; Marmar et al., 1994). This questionnaire has shown excellent internal consistency (α = .94). Participants were instructed to answer each of the 10 items in reference to their biopsy results disclosure event. Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all true) to 5 (extremely true), with possible scores ranging from 0 to 50. Higher scores reflect greater peritraumatic dissociation.

sec.title: Data analyses
sec.p: The present study employed a mixed-method approach in which qualitative narrative data were first coded, and frequencies of narrative features were used to examine their association with subsequent psychological distress outcomes using regression analyses (Creswell & Clark, 2017).

sec.title: Qualitative
sec.p: Narrative analyses. Narrative transcripts were analysed using a deductive content analysis approach, with narrative features coded according to a theory-driven framework grounded in autobiographical memory theory (Rubin & Umanath, 2015) and related narrative models. To ensure coding reliability, two initial calibration rounds were conducted. A first narrative was coded and discussed collectively to refine definitions. After updating the coding manual, a second narrative was independently rated by all four coders [JF, LH, RL, AP] to confirm coding consistency. Once this process was complete, the remaining narratives were randomly assigned to coding pairs, with each pair including at least one of the two interviewers [JF; AP] to ensure accurate interpretation of auditory and paralinguistic features (e.g. emotional changes in voice). Coders were blind to participants’ psychological distress scores (Bisson Desrochers et al., 2016), and all coding was conducted independently prior to any consensus meetings. For frequency-based codes, which were counted per code within each narrative and typically ranged from 0 to 50, an acceptable inter-rater agreement threshold was set at a maximum standard deviation of 3 between coders’ scores. This corresponds to approximately 6% of the maximum possible value and is consistent with methodological recommendations for qualitative coding frameworks (Guest et al., 2011; Syed & Nelson, 2015). When this threshold was exceeded for a given code, a discussion was initiated to reach consensus. The same coding framework was applied to both the baseline autobiographical events and biopsy results disclosure narratives, except for the recall frequency ‘Cancer-related words’ code (form), which was not applicable to baseline narratives prior to result disclosure. For baseline narratives, frequency-based codes were adjusted by dividing the total count by the number of reported events (ranging in our sample from 2 to 4) to obtain a proportional index of recall tendencies.

sec.title: Quantitative
sec.p: All quantitative analyses were performed using R statistical software (version 4.3.1).

Descriptive analyses of the sample. Descriptive analyses were conducted to summarize the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the sample. Continuous variables are reported using means, standard deviations, and ranges, while categorical variables are summarized using frequencies and percentages.

Preliminary analyses of narrative features. Narrative features according to memory type (baseline autobiographical events vs. biopsy results disclosure event) and diagnostic outcome (positive vs. negative). Composite scores were computed for each narrative dimension (emotional intensity, centrality, and recall frequency) and for each narrative level (content and form). Paired-sample t-tests were used to compare the composite scores of cancer disclosure narratives with those of baseline narratives across each dimension, while Welch’s unequal variances t-tests assessed whether these scores differed according to participants’ diagnosis status. These analyses aimed to determine whether the biopsy results-related narrative was distinct from general autobiographical memories and whether its narrative features varied as a function of diagnosis before testing their association with later psychological distress.

Analyses examining the association with psychological distress. Associations between narrative characteristics and psychological distress were examined using two distinct sets of linear regressions. Participants receiving positive and negative biopsy results were analysed as a single group, as the sample size was insufficient to reliably examine between-group differences. This approach was also considered appropriate given previous evidence showing that clinically significant psychological distress may occur following both positive and negative biopsy results (Fortin, Paquin, et al., 2025). Composite-level models were run separately for content and form. In a second, independent set of models, individual code-level analyses were conducted to assess the unique association of each narrative characteristic with psychological distress. Analyses (composite-level only) were conducted using baseline autobiographical narratives to verify whether observed associations were specific to the biopsy results disclosure event rather than to general autobiographical memory characteristics. Including all narrative variables in a single multivariate model would have reduced statistical power and increased the risk of overfitting given the limited sample size (Bender & Lange, 2001; Rothman, 1990). In all regression models, self-reported peritraumatic dissociation at disclosure (PDEQ-10SRV) was included as a covariate, given its established role as an acute reaction known to influence memory consolidation (Bedard-Gilligan & Zoellner, 2012) and later distress (Bedard-Gilligan & Zoellner, 2012; Werner & Griffin, 2012).

sec.title: Descriptive analyses of the sample
sec.p: Seventy-one participants took part in the interviews, although three participants were excluded from the analyses. For one, the audio recording was not sufficiently intelligible to allow for reliable transcription and coding. The other participant did not respond to the interview question as intended, instead using the opportunity to discuss broader issues within the healthcare system. In the third case, the participant invited her husband to join the interview while answering the key question; as he contributed details from his own perspective, it was not possible to determine whether the account reflected her memory or their shared recollection.

sec.title: Descriptive qualitative and quantitative analyses of narrative features
sec.p: As expected, paired-sample t-tests indicated that, across all narrative dimensions (emotional intensity, centrality, and recall frequency), composite scores from the baseline autobiographical narratives were significantly lower than those from the biopsy results disclosure narratives. In contrast, Welch’s unequal variances t-tests revealed no significant differences in baseline autobiographical narratives composite scores between participants with a positive versus negative diagnosis (see Supplemental for more details).

In biopsy results disclosure analyses, Welch’s unequal variances t-tests revealed that participants with a positive diagnosis showed higher scores for centrality in both content, t(41.67) = 2.17, p = .036, and form, t(42.36) = 2.35, p = .024, compared to those with a negative diagnosis. No significant differences were found for the other composite scores (see Supplemental for more details). Moreover, narrative features included both content and form-related codes reflecting the thematic, structural, and emotional properties of participants’ autobiographical accounts. sec.title: Quantitative analyses
sec.p:
While controlling for self-reported dissociation 24 h following the biopsy results, linear regressions using composite scores revealed that, within content, composite scores of centrality were significantly associated with PTSS (B = .878, 95% CI [0.154, 1.602]) but not with non-specific distress (B = .053, 95% CI [−0.078, 0.183]), emotional intensity was associated with both PTSS (B = .601, 95% CI [0.233, 0.968]) and non-specific distress (B = .085, 95% CI [0.020, 0.150]). Recall frequency showed no statistically significant association with either distress outcome, though a substantial association cannot be ruled out given the wide confidence intervals observed (PTSS: B = .203, 95% CI [−2.036, 2.442]; non-specific distress: B = .024, 95% CI [−0.366, 0.414]). Analyses of individual content codes further indicated that features related to centrality and emotional intensity were associated with PTSS, while only emotional intensity was associated with non-specific distress. Within form, composite scores of emotional intensity showed no substantial evidence of an association with PTSS (B = .031, 95% CI [−0.055, 0.116]) or non-specific distress (B = .012, 95% CI [−0.002, 0.026]). Analyses of individual form codes showed that all three dimensions (centrality, emotional intensity, and recall frequency) were significantly associated with PTSS, whereas only recall frequency was significantly associated with non-specific distress (see Table 3). sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The present mixed-method study examined whether and how recall frequency, emotional intensity, and centrality of autobiographical narratives collected on average 7 days post-biopsy result disclosure were associated with psychological distress 1 month later, while controlling for self-report dissociation. Findings showed that for biopsy results disclosure narrative content, higher emotional intensity and greater centrality were associated with higher psychological distress scores as initially hypothesized, whereas recall frequency showed no statistically significant association, contrary to the initial hypothesis, though wide confidence intervals preclude firm conclusions about the absence of an effect. Regarding narrative form, recall frequency, emotional intensity and centrality were each associated with psychological distress one-month post-biopsy results in line with the initial hypothesis. These associations were not observed for baseline autobiographical memories, showing that the associations found between narrative features and psychological distress are specific to the biopsy results disclosure event.

For narrative content, emotional intensity was associated with both PTSS and non-specific distress, with the largest number of significant subcodes linked to PTSS, whereas centrality was uniquely linked to PTSS. This pattern suggests that intense emotional encoding may reflect a broader emotional vulnerability following positive or negative biopsy results, while a heightened sense of centrality indicates that the event has become integrated into one’s self-concept in a way characteristic of trauma-related meaning-making. Centrality scores were higher among participants who received a positive biopsy result, suggesting that receiving a breast cancer diagnosis may anchor the event more deeply within one’s life narrative. Narratives reflecting high centrality often involved statements that placed the biopsy disclosure as a defining moment or turning point in participants’ life stories, sometimes accompanied by disorganized or circular reflections suggesting ongoing attempts at integration (see Table 2). Such central positioning of the cancer experience may strengthen intrusive recall and self-referential processing, mechanisms more specific to post-traumatic reactions than to non-specific distress (Berntsen & Rubin, 2006). Recall frequency showed no statistically significant association with any psychological distress symptom in our sample, though the wide confidence intervals observed suggest this finding should be interpreted with caution. In prior studies, recall frequency was a strong predictor of post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms primarily among participants already diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and assessed at later time points (at least one month post-event), when intrusive recollections are more likely to be salient (Rubin et al., 2008). Moreover, in the present study, recall frequency was coded from participants’ free recall of the disclosure of the experience, whereas some other studies assessed it through self-report questionnaires that directly ask how often the memory of the traumatic event comes to mind (e.g. Ayers et al., 2015; Bisson Desrochers et al., 2016). In a preventive context, however, it may be more appropriate to capture recall indirectly through free narration, since directly probing how often the memory comes to mind may be psychologically demanding and subject to recall bias (Mamat & Anderson, 2023). In contrast, free recall provides a more naturalistic window into how the memory is spontaneously represented, whereas cued recalls, more common in clinical PTSD settings, are typically used to guide treatment rather than to identify early predictors (see review: Falsetti et al., 2002). Together, these temporal and methodological distinctions may partly explain the discrepancy between the current findings and prior evidence. Another explanation could be the possibility that memory recall frequency, particularly when assessed shortly after the event, reflects a normative cognitive response rather than a pathological one (Figueiredo et al., 2004). In non-acute narrative studies where post-traumatic stress disorder is already diagnosed, recall frequency may serve more as a marker of ongoing distress rather than a predictor. Yet, during the early post-event phase, as in the current study, frequent recall (e.g. discussing the upcoming biopsy results with others) may still represent adaptive processing. This suggests that the recall dimension could be more indicative of chronicity or symptom consolidation, rather than early vulnerability. For narrative form, all three assessed dimensions, emotional intensity, centrality, and recall frequency, were associated with psychological distress, which was consistent with the initial hypothesis and aligned with autobiographical memory theory (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Rubin et al., 2008). As in other contexts of highly stressful or potentially traumatic events, this pattern highlights the role of heightened emotional expression in memory. It is relevant because beyond the content of what is recalled, the way memory is expressed throughout self-focused language, verbal fillers or repeated references to cancer, may serve as a cross-cutting marker of psychological vulnerability in individuals recalling the disclosure of their breast biopsy results.

These results support the idea that receiving a medical diagnosis, regardless of whether it confirms cancer or not, can be encoded and recalled in similar ways to highly stressful or potentially traumatic autobiographical events. Although life-threatening medical diagnoses are no longer classified as traumatic events under the DSM-5 criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), our findings suggest that diagnosis disclosure may activate similar cognitive and emotional processes to those observed in trauma-related memory, even in non-pathological or non-life-threatening contexts. Unlike typical post-traumatic stress disorder contexts that revolve around a single circumscribed event (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), diagnosis disclosure occurs within an ongoing medical trajectory, yet the present findings suggest that this moment may serve as an autobiographical anchor. Importantly, the narrative features observed at this stage did not appear to reflect a stable dispositional style, but rather a context-specific response to the emotional salience of the disclosure event. This difference between baseline autobiographical memory and highly stressful autobiographical memory is also found in post-traumatic stress disorder studies, where trauma-related memories become more central, emotionally intense, and distinct from other autobiographical memories (e.g. Berntsen & Rubin, 2006; Rubin & Umanath, 2015). Observing a comparable pattern in individuals who had not developed PTSD highlights that the cognitive and emotional mechanisms underlying trauma-related memory formation can emerge early in the adjustment process, becoming active in the immediate aftermath of a highly stressful event, before a pathological trajectory is established. The present findings also align with Rubin et al.’s (2008; 2015) theoretical model, which emphasizes memory features (emotional intensity, centrality, retrieval frequency) as key mechanisms linking stressful experiences to psychological outcomes. Within the early phases of the breast cancer trajectory, biopsy result disclosure may consolidate as a salient memory that temporarily reshapes self-referential processing while simultaneously competing with ongoing medical and personal stressors (Fortin, Rudd, et al., 2025). How this specific event is later recalled thus offers a critical lens for understanding memory processes under strain that can inform preventive intervention rather than post-trauma repair.

Moreover, while the Distress Thermometer is commonly used in oncology care (Blenkiron et al., 2014), our results indicate that certain narrative features, particularly those linked to centrality (content and form) and emotional intensity (form) may reflect distress profiles not fully captured by this single tool. When such trauma-relevant features emerge in patients’ discourse, more integrative screening instruments, including PTSS, may be warranted. Relying solely on a global non-specific distress score risks overlooking patients who do not meet the threshold yet still struggle with clinically meaningful symptoms. In this way, incorporating narrative markers, such as the strong emotions expressed, the way patients describe the impact of the results on their sense of self and future, and the recurrence of cancer-related themes, alongside existing tools could refine screening practices at least one-week post-disclosure. These markers may help differentiate non-specific distress from trauma-related symptom profiles, allowing clinicians to intervene earlier and tailor support more precisely.

sec.title: Limitations and future directions
sec.p: A limitation of this study is that the disclosure of biopsy results was not always recalled by participants as a discrete or isolated event. In many narratives, patients spontaneously referred to experiences leading up to the disclosure (e.g. the biopsy procedure itself) or to subsequent medical encounters and uncertainties about the future. This suggests that, within the breast cancer trajectory, distress cannot be attributed solely to the moment of diagnosis, but should be understood as part of a prolonged and multifaceted process. It is also possible that, for some participants, other moments related to the diagnosis process (e.g. the biopsy procedure, waiting period, or subsequent medical consultations) were experienced as equally or more salient than the disclosure itself. Accordingly, the present findings highlight memory and distress related to the disclosure while acknowledging that they are embedded in a broader sequence of medical stressors. In these cases (19.12%; 13/68 participants), coding was applied to the participant’s full recollection elicited by the disclosure prompt, potentially capturing aspects of the broader cancer experience beyond the disclosure event itself. Another limitation is that participants’ psychological distress on the day of the interview was not assessed. It is therefore not possible to rule out their potential influence on how the event was recalled. Although the psychological distress questionnaire was sent to participants approximately seven days after disclosure in the larger study, the timing of completion varied considerably across individuals, limiting its usefulness as an indicator of emotional state during the interview. In this regard, it is not possible to determine whether, or to what extent, momentary affect contributed to the narratives collected in the present study and to the symptoms collected one month later. Moreover, participation in the narrative interview was optional within the larger longitudinal study. Consequently, although participants included in the present study were mostly similar to the broader study sample on sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, participants included in the present analyses may represent a subgroup of patients who were particularly willing or available to verbally recount their experience, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings. A further limitation is that the relatively small sample size, particularly for the quantitative analyses, may have limited statistical power to detect smaller associations and should be considered when interpreting non-significant findings. Future studies with larger cohorts should estimate integrative statistical models that include all narrative dimensions simultaneously and examine whether associations differ according to biopsy outcome, as the present sample could not accommodate these approaches. Such analyses would clarify both the relative contribution of emotional intensity, recall frequency, and centrality, and the potential moderating role of positive versus negative biopsy results in the breast cancer context.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study demonstrates that how individuals recall and communicate their memory of the breast biopsy result disclosure (as assessed seven days post-diagnosis) is associated with psychological distress up to one month later. Specifically, narrative dimensions such as centrality, emotional intensity, and recall frequency were associated with PTSS and non-specific distress. By highlighting associations between autobiographical memory features and subsequent psychological distress, this study suggests a promising avenue for future research examining the potential role of narrative characteristics in identifying psychological vulnerability during the breast cancer trajectory.
